row.basis: praising the name; the name exalted
row.note: The opening command to glorify the Lord's name meets the psalm's call to praise YHWH's name because his name alone is exalted; the psalm joins the act of praise to the name's height.

row.basis: called by name; “you are mine”
row.note: The commentary reads the Lord's name as a sign of ownership and distinction; here YHWH calls Jacob by name and declares Israel his, making naming an explicit claim of belonging.

row.basis: writes YHWH on the hand
row.note: The commentary's “name as an identifying mark” is literalized when a person writes YHWH on his hand and claims the name Israel; the verse presents the mark as chosen allegiance.

row.basis: engraved holiness on the priest's forehead
row.note: A gold plate engraved “Holy to YHWH” is worn on Aaron's forehead; the bodily inscription identifies sacred service and makes concrete the commentary's hearing of the Lord's name as a distinguishing mark.

row.basis: God's name placed upon Israel
row.note: The priests “put” YHWH's name upon Israel and God blesses them; this is a direct name-as-belonging-sign parallel to the commentary's gloss of the Lord as owner and the name as his mark.

row.basis: covenant sign in the flesh
row.note: Circumcision is explicitly called a covenant sign “in your flesh”; this gives the commentary's skin-mark scene a concrete covenantal counterpart that distinguishes a community through a bodily sign.

row.basis: Sabbath as a sign between YHWH and Israel
row.note: The Sabbath is a sign between God and Israel, by which they know that YHWH sanctifies them; it connects a religious act with a visible community identity and holiness, as the commentary connects remembrance and prayer with the Lord's mark.

row.basis: blood sign on the houses
row.note: The blood on the doorways is a sign by which YHWH distinguishes Israelite houses and spares them; it shows a mark identifying whose household is under protection, while the commentary also gives marks opposite fates.

row.basis: sign on hand; memorial of deliverance
row.note: The exodus instruction makes the remembered law a sign on the hand and a memorial between the eyes; it brings bodily marking together with remembering the Lord's deliverance, a specific ritual counterpart to the commentary's name-and-remembrance reading.

row.basis: pierced ear; lifelong service
row.note: When a servant chooses to remain with his master, his ear is pierced and he stays for life; a chosen attachment leaves a bodily trace that identifies an enduring relation, matching the commentary's claim that preference leaves a mark.

row.basis: forehead mark distinguishes mourners
row.note: Before Jerusalem's slaughter, a mark is placed on the foreheads of those grieving its abominations so they are passed over; this is a precise counter-role to the stigmatizing brand in the commentary's Q 68 scene: a mark can distinguish and spare.

row.basis: Arabic ism / Hebrew shem, “name”
row.note: The frozen commentary labels Q 87:1's word “name” under a disputed w-s-m branch. Hebrew shem here is YHWH's enduring self-designation and memorial across generations; the name-word correspondence is a possible Semitic cognate, without validating the commentary's debated branding etymology.

row.basis: hidden things and good or evil judged
row.note: The verse says God brings every deed, including every hidden thing, into judgment, whether good or evil; it closely joins the commentary's “knows the hidden” clause to its reading of traces that reveal good and evil.

row.basis: word known before it is spoken
row.note: The psalm says YHWH knows a word before it reaches the speaker's tongue; this specifies divine knowledge of what is concealed behind public speech, as in the commentary's open/hidden pairing.

row.basis: face versus heart
row.note: Humans see outward appearance, but YHWH sees the heart; beside the commentary's readable marks on faces and its claim that God knows what is hidden, this warns that an exterior sign and inward state are not identical.

row.basis: Cain's protective mark
row.note: YHWH puts a sign on Cain so that anyone who finds him will not kill him; unlike the humiliating brand in the commentary's Q 68 example, this bodily sign protects a marked offender.

row.basis: seal on heart and arm
row.note: The lover asks to be set as a seal on heart and arm, a durable bodily claim of love; it offers a distinct intimate use of the commentary's seal-like mark, binding the marked person to another.

row.basis: fire and sulfur on Sodom
row.note: Genesis tells the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah by fire and sulfur; it is the Torah narrative behind the commentary's appeal to the ruined Lot-city as a readable sign.

row.basis: cities overthrown
row.note: The cities and surrounding plain are overthrown in the Lot narrative, directly matching the commentary's scene of the settlements turned upside down and supplying the story's own account of the ruin later read as a sign.

row.basis: smoke rising from the destroyed land
row.note: Abraham looks toward Sodom and sees smoke rising like smoke from a furnace; the visible aftermath is a trace by which a witness can recognize what happened, close to the commentary's readers of ruined places.

row.basis: smoking wasteland; pillar of salt as memorial
row.note: Wisdom retells Lot's escape and describes the cities' smoking waste and the salt pillar as a monument to an unbelieving soul; it makes the remains themselves evidence of the event, illuminating the commentary's “signs for those who read” the ruined site.

row.basis: failure left as a reminder that cannot be hidden
row.note: Wisdom says those who rejected wisdom failed to recognize good and left a memorial of folly so their failures could not remain hidden; this interprets the surviving ruin as a trace that teaches later observers, closely matching the commentary's reading of signs in a destroyed place.

row.basis: forced ivy mark of Dionysus
row.note: Ptolemy's decree brands Jews with Dionysus's ivy symbol and reduces them to a subjected status; this makes a bodily mark an imposed religious-identity sign, unlike the individual punitive nose brand in the commentary. Verse wording and numbering can vary by edition.

row.basis: Ezekiel's forehead marks; ink and blood
row.note: The rabbis read Ezekiel's mark as different signs for righteous and wicked, then debate the hidden failure of the righteous to protest; this connects bodily signs with God's knowledge of concealed moral responsibility, complicating the mark's simple protective role.

row.basis: tattoo as writing; Rabbi Shimon's name condition
row.note: The Mishnah discusses Lev 19:28's tattoo ban and Rabbi Shimon's view that liability requires writing a name; it makes the content of a skin mark, specifically a name, matter alongside the commentary's name/brand association.

row.basis: prohibition on incisions and tattoos
row.note: Leviticus forbids gashing the flesh for the dead and tattoo marks; against the commentary's pious trace of prostration and punitive brand, it supplies a distinct Israelite boundary on inscribing the body.

row.basis: Biblical Aramaic nûr, “fire”; furnace for image-refusal
row.note: The commentary labels the source root of Qur'anic al-nār as n-w-r and develops fire as a camel brand; Biblical Aramaic nûr in Daniel names the furnace imposed on those who refuse the king's image. The cognate fire-word appears in a scene where worship allegiance carries a fiery penalty, though Daniel's furnace is not a brand.

row.basis: law written on the heart
row.note: YHWH writes the covenant instruction on the people's hearts; this gives an inward, lasting inscription alongside the commentary's bodily mark and its claim that a person's chosen relation leaves a trace.

row.basis: shepherd calls his own sheep by name
row.note: The shepherd calls his own sheep by name and leads them out; the passage joins naming with ownership and recognition, directly clarifying the commentary's interpretation of the Lord's name as a sign of whose something is.

row.basis: bought with a price; glorify God in the body
row.note: Paul says believers were bought and therefore must glorify God in their bodies; this brings the commentary's owner-mark reading of glorifying the Lord's name onto the body itself, while using ethical language rather than a brand.

row.basis: God's seal; the Lord knows his own
row.note: The verse describes God's foundation as bearing a seal: the Lord knows those who are his, and those who name the Lord must turn from wrongdoing. It unites name, ownership, distinguishing knowledge, and keeping the sign morally clean, closely matching the commentary's developed reading.

row.basis: Father's and Lamb's names on foreheads
row.note: The Lamb's followers bear the names of the Father and Lamb on their foreheads; this is a direct image of divine names as visible belonging marks, corresponding to the commentary's name-as-owner-sign and its facial traces of worship.

row.basis: beast's mark and worship
row.note: The angel warns against worshiping the beast and receiving its mark on forehead or hand; like the commentary's contrast between the Lord's name and a hostile mark, this sign identifies a rival allegiance, though the source's punitive brand is aimed at a denier rather than a worshiping community.

row.basis: fire for those marked and worshiping
row.note: The next verse makes the marked beast-worshiper's fate torment in fire and sulfur; Revelation thus explicitly joins the mark and fire that the commentary sets as opposed traces, with a different allegiance determining the outcome.

row.basis: mark/name/number as trade credential
row.note: The mark, beast's name, or number is required to buy or sell; this adds the mark's public social function as a way to identify and separate people, beyond its bodily placement.

row.basis: marks of Jesus on Paul's body
row.note: Paul says he bears Jesus's marks on his body; these scars identify the allegiance and service that have left a trace, offering a Christian bodily-mark counterpart distinct from a branded animal or punitive stigma.

row.basis: nail marks as bodily evidence
row.note: Thomas demands to see the mark of the nails and the wound in Jesus's side; the wounds are bodily traces used to recognize the crucified person, paralleling the commentary's claim that a mark on a body can be read.

row.basis: washed face during fasting
row.note: Jesus tells the fasting person to wash and anoint the face so the fast is not displayed to others, while the Father sees in secret; this offers a contrary reading to the commentary's visible prostration mark by locating devotional recognition in concealed practice.

row.basis: known by fruits
row.note: Jesus says people are recognized by their fruits; the produced result functions as a readable trace of the source, matching the commentary's explanation of athar as what remains and its claim that good and evil can be discerned from a mark.

row.basis: fruitless tree thrown into fire
row.note: The bad tree that fails to make good fruit is cut down and thrown into fire; this uniquely joins the commentary's readable good/bad trace with its other image of fire as the fate of the rejected.

row.basis: hidden things brought to light
row.note: Jesus says hidden things are destined to be disclosed; the verse concerns eventual revelation rather than God's present omniscience, but it connects the commentary's hidden trace with its public/hidden distinction.

row.basis: nothing hidden; all laid bare before God
row.note: No creature is hidden from God's sight and all is exposed before the one to whom account is given; this develops the commentary's statement that God knows the open and hidden and that traces can disclose a person's condition.

row.basis: circumcision of heart by the Spirit
row.note: Paul interprets true circumcision as inward, of the heart and Spirit rather than letter; this re-reads the fleshly covenant sign of Genesis 17 and brings an invisible moral trace beside the commentary's literal brand and outward prayer mark.

row.basis: seen transient; unseen eternal
row.note: Paul contrasts what is seen and temporary with what is unseen and eternal; this meets both the commentary's visible/invisible trace and its contrast between preferred worldly life and the more enduring hereafter.

row.basis: world passing; God's will remains forever
row.note: The world and its desires pass away, while the one doing God's will remains forever; this directly answers the commentary's “you prefer worldly life” beside “the hereafter is better and more lasting.”

row.basis: earthly treasure destroyed
row.note: Jesus warns that earthly treasure is vulnerable to moth and decay; this gives a concrete instance of the worldly life that does not endure, setting up the commentary's contrast with the lasting hereafter.

row.basis: treasure in heaven not destroyed
row.note: Heavenly treasure cannot be destroyed or stolen; this is a concrete counterpart to the commentary's claim that the hereafter is better and more enduring than worldly life.

row.basis: heart follows its treasure
row.note: Jesus says the heart is where one's treasure is; it links preference to an inward mark or orientation, specifying how what one values identifies the person.

row.basis: Moses chooses hardship over sin's fleeting pleasure
row.note: Moses chooses mistreatment with God's people over temporary enjoyment in sin; the passage gives a concrete reversal of preferring present worldly life and shows a chosen allegiance that shapes a life.

row.basis: reproach accepted for future reward
row.note: Moses considers disgrace for the anointed greater wealth than Egypt's treasures because he looks to the reward; it explicitly links choosing what is lasting with what is better, echoing the commentary's contrast of worldly preference and the enduring hereafter.

row.basis: work disclosed and tested by fire
row.note: Each one's work becomes manifest at the Day and is tested by fire; this joins the commentary's residue that distinguishes a person with its fire image, as actions are exposed and their quality shown.

row.basis: Sodom reduced to ashes as an example
row.note: Peter says God reduced Sodom and Gomorrah to ashes and made them an example of what awaits the ungodly; it interprets the Lot-city's destruction as a readable warning, complementing the commentary's signs in the ruined site.

row.basis: Sodom as example of punishment by eternal fire
row.note: Jude presents Sodom and neighboring cities as an example by undergoing punishment of eternal fire; the Christian interpretation makes the destroyed place a sign of the future fiery fate, joining the commentary's readable ruins and Great Fire.

row.basis: misuse of YHWH's name
row.note: The command forbids bearing YHWH's name falsely and says the guilty will not be acquitted; it gives a concrete ethical counterpart to the commentary's secondary hearing of glorifying the name as keeping the Lord's identifying mark free from fault.

row.basis: blasphemy of the Name
row.note: The narrative identifies a man who blasphemes and curses the Name; this directly intersects the commentary's concern for the Lord's name and its account of a denier whose contemptuous speech earns a bodily stigma.

row.basis: penalty for blaspheming the Name
row.note: The same law sentences the blasphemer of YHWH's name to death; it adds a concrete sanction for dishonoring the name beside the commentary's punitive mark for dismissing revelation.

row.basis: sanctifying a profaned name
row.note: YHWH says he will sanctify his great name, which Israel profaned among the nations; this directly develops the commentary's secondary sense of keeping the Lord's name-mark free of blemish, and makes public reputation part of the issue.

row.basis: nose and ears cut; survivors consumed by fire
row.note: In the allegory of Jerusalem and Samaria's infidelity, enemies mutilate the women's faces and the remnant is consumed by fire; it supplies a concrete judgment-image of facial stigma joined to fire, while the context and instrument differ from the commentary's brand.

row.basis: Abel's blood cries from the ground
row.note: Cain's hidden murder is disclosed when Abel's blood cries to God from the ground; this is a specific trace left on earth that reveals an act and its agent, enriching the commentary's claim that an effect can remain visible or unseen.

row.basis: Zion engraved on God's palms
row.note: YHWH says Zion is engraved on his palms and continually before him; this reverses the commentary's owner-mark image, showing the marked person preserved in the owner's memory, and adds permanence to the trace.

row.basis: forehead plate and acceptance of offerings
row.note: Aaron bears the guilt attached to the sacred gifts on the forehead plate so the offerings may be accepted; this continuation gives the inscribed holiness a cleansing and acceptance function beside the commentary's call to keep the Lord's mark pure.

row.basis: no hiding place from YHWH
row.note: YHWH asks whether anyone can hide where he cannot see and says he fills heaven and earth; it directly specifies that concealed conduct remains within divine sight, as in the commentary's public/hidden pair.

row.basis: God reveals hidden things and knows darkness
row.note: Daniel's prayer says God reveals deep and hidden things and knows what is in darkness; this supplies a close biblical-Aramaic formulation of divine knowledge of the concealed alongside the commentary's explicit open/hidden clause.

row.basis: book of remembrance for those who esteem YHWH's name
row.note: A book of remembrance is written for those who fear YHWH and esteem his name; it makes devotion leave a durable written trace and connects remembrance of the name with later recognition.

row.basis: distinction between the righteous and the wicked
row.note: The audience will again see a distinction between the righteous and wicked, between one who serves God and one who does not; this specifies the commentary's claim that a mark distinguishes one person from another by the allegiance it records.

row.basis: book of the covenant read aloud
row.note: Moses reads the book of the covenant to Israel, who answer to its words; this gives a concrete scriptural witness for the commentary's contrast between dismissing ancient accounts as tales and receiving the earliest writings as revelation.

row.basis: Moses' scroll kept as a witness
row.note: Moses orders the written law to be placed beside the ark as a witness against Israel; this directly illuminates the surah's appeal to the scrolls of Moses after the commentary's denier labels the stories of the ancients fables.

row.basis: Lot's wife becomes a pillar of salt
row.note: During the escape from Sodom, Lot's wife becomes a pillar of salt; this is an individual bodily remnant within the same destruction story, later read in Wisdom 10:7 as a memorial, adding a concrete trace beside the commentary's ruined-city signs.

row.basis: secret speech is not hidden
row.note: Wisdom says every utterance is heard and no secret whisper escapes; this gives a Jewish formulation of concealed speech remaining knowable, particularly apt beside the commentary's open/hidden knowledge and its judged denier's words.

row.basis: people inscribed and sealed for life or death
row.note: The rabbinic judgment tradition pictures books opened and the wholly righteous sealed for life, the wholly wicked for death; it interprets a written mark as distinguishing moral status and fate, extending the commentary's identity-mark contrast into an eschatological register.

row.basis: Christ's letter written on hearts and read by all
row.note: Paul calls the community a letter of Christ, written by the Spirit on human hearts and known and read by everyone; this is an inward trace that identifies its source and can be read, directly developing the commentary's mark-and-recognition relation.

row.basis: God's seal and Spirit in hearts
row.note: Paul says God set his seal on believers and gave the Spirit in their hearts as a pledge; this specifies an inward divine mark of belonging and a lasting guarantee, distinct from the name-inscription in the commentary.

row.basis: circumcision interpreted as a seal of faith
row.note: Paul calls Abraham's circumcision a sign and seal of the righteousness of faith he already had; this Christian reading interprets the fleshly sign in Genesis 17 as certifying an inward allegiance, adding a distinct meaning to the commentary's mark of ownership.

row.basis: God's servants sealed on their foreheads before harm
row.note: The servants of God receive a seal on their foreheads before the earth is harmed; besides Revelation 14's names of belonging, this mark specifically distinguishes and protects a community before destruction, like Ezekiel's spared mourners.

row.basis: account for every careless word at judgment
row.note: Jesus says people will give account on judgment day for every careless word; this connects the commentary's denier's spoken dismissal and God's knowledge of the open and hidden with a verbal trace that carries consequences.

row.basis: words justify or condemn
row.note: Jesus says a person is justified or condemned by their words; this adds the words' role as evidence that distinguishes a person's standing, alongside the commentary's punishment of one who calls revelation ancient fables.

row.basis: hidden heart-counsels disclosed; praise from God
row.note: At the Lord's coming, hidden things of darkness and heart-counsels are brought to light, and each receives praise from God; this joins concealed traces, divine recognition, and moral evaluation in a way close to the commentary's open/hidden knowledge.

row.basis: one tongue blesses God and curses people
row.note: James says the tongue blesses the Lord and Father yet curses people made in God's likeness; it gives a specific ethical test for honoring God's name, relevant to the commentary's contrast between glorifying the Lord and contemptuous speech.

row.basis: gain the world and forfeit oneself
row.note: Jesus asks what profit there is in gaining the whole world while losing or forfeiting oneself; this sharply reverses preference for worldly life and specifies its cost beside the commentary's better, lasting hereafter.

row.basis: sowing to flesh or Spirit yields corruption or eternal life
row.note: Paul says sowing to flesh reaps corruption while sowing to the Spirit reaps eternal life; the harvested result is a trace of one's chosen orientation, directly linking preference, remainder, and lasting fate.

row.basis: fruit of former conduct ends in death
row.note: Paul asks what fruit came from former shameful practices and says their end is death; the fruit is a readable remainder of chosen conduct, tied to the fate that contrasts with the commentary's lasting hereafter.

row.basis: fruit of holiness and end of eternal life
row.note: Freed from sin and enslaved to God, believers bear fruit for holiness whose end is eternal life; this combines the commentary's owner relation, trace of action, and lasting destiny in one passage.

row.basis: acts toward the least counted as acts toward the king
row.note: In the judgment scene, care for the least is counted as service to the king; deeds become the trace by which allegiance is recognized, giving a concrete ethical counterpart to the commentary's claim that preference leaves an identifying mark.

row.basis: eternal punishment and eternal life
row.note: The judgment ends with the two groups sent to eternal punishment or eternal life; this supplies a specific Christian formulation of the commentary's contrast between the fire-bound and the better, enduring hereafter.

row.basis: books opened; the dead judged by their deeds
row.note: The dead are judged according to their deeds recorded in opened books; this turns the commentary's trace into an eschatological record that exposes and distinguishes each person's conduct.

row.basis: name absent from the book of life; lake of fire
row.note: Anyone not found written in the book of life is thrown into the lake of fire; this explicitly makes a written name the mark distinguishing the saved from those assigned to fire, uniting the commentary's owner-sign and fire images.
